q: During the First World War, the nationalist response in India was three-fold. Which of the following correctly describes the position of the Extremists, including Tilak?
o: They demanded immediate complete independence as a precondition for any cooperation
They organised armed uprisings against British forces stationed in India
They supported the war effort, mistakenly believing Britain would reward India's loyalty with self-government
They completely boycotted all war-related activity

q: Tilak's Indian Home Rule League, set up in April 1916 with its headquarters at Poona, operated in which regions?
o: All of India including Bombay city
Only Bengal and Bihar
Maharashtra (excluding Bombay city), Karnataka, Central Provinces and Berar
Only Punjab and Sindh

q: Annie Besant's All-India Home Rule League, set up in September 1916 in Madras with George Arundale as organising secretary, had how many branches, and covered which area?
o: 200 branches, covering the rest of India including Bombay city
10 branches, covering only Punjab
50 branches, covering only Bengal
Six branches, covering only Madras Presidency

q: Which of the following sections of Indian society is noted in the chapter as largely NOT joining the Home Rule agitation, fearing it would mean Hindu (especially upper-caste) majority rule?
o: Educated middle-class professionals
Students in Madras and Bombay
Most Muslims, Anglo-Indians, and non-Brahmins from the South
Moderate Congressmen disillusioned with Congress inactivity

q: Montagu, the Secretary of State for India, made a striking comment comparing the effect of interning Annie Besant to which mythological reference?
o: Ravana's ten heads multiplying with each cut
Hanuman's growing form when confronted
Krishna's Sudarshan Chakra returning to strike back
Shiva cutting his wife into fifty-two pieces only to discover he had fifty-two wives

q: Annie Besant was released from detention in:
o: September 1917
June 1917

q: Which of the following is cited as a positive, long-term contribution of the Home Rule Movement to the freedom struggle?
o: It eliminated all communal tensions between Hindus and Muslims
It immediately achieved full self-government for India
It shifted the movement's emphasis from the educated elite to the masses and created an organisational link between town and country
It replaced the Indian National Congress entirely with the Home Rule Leagues

q: The Lucknow Session of the Indian National Congress (1916), presided over by Ambika Charan Majumdar, is significant chiefly for:
o: The founding of the Indian National Congress itself
The declaration of Purna Swaraj as the Congress goal
Readmitting the Extremists led by Tilak to the Congress fold and the signing of the Lucknow Pact with the Muslim League
The launch of the Non-Cooperation Movement

q: According to the chapter's critical assessment, the Congress's acceptance of separate electorates in the Lucknow Pact represented:
o: The complete elimination of minority fears about majority domination
A rejection of any communal basis for representation
A temporary measure immediately reversed at the next Congress session
A major landmark in the evolution of the Muslim League's two-nation theory, since Congress and League came together as separate political entities

q: Maulana Azad's journal Al Hilal and Mohammad Ali's journal Comrade, both suppressed during World War I, reflected the anti-imperialist sentiments of which group within the Muslim League?
o: The Ahmadiyya movement
The Deoband ulema exclusively
The younger 'Young Party' Muslims turning towards bolder nationalist politics
The Aligarh school loyal to the British government

q: The Calcutta session of the Muslim League (1912) committed the League to:
o: Working with other groups for a system of self-government suited to India, provided it did not conflict with protecting Muslim interests
Complete rejection of any cooperation with the Indian National Congress
Unconditional loyalty to British rule with no self-government demand
Support for a fully separate Muslim state

q: Edwin Samuel Montagu's statement of August 20, 1917 (the 'August Declaration') in the British House of Commons announced government policy towards:
o: Immediate grant of full independence to India
Permanent continuation of Company-style administration
Increasing Indian participation in administration and the progressive realisation of responsible self-government within the British Empire
Abolition of separate electorates

q: Which of the following distinguishes Montagu's 1917 statement from Lord Morley's earlier position on constitutional reform (in the context of the 1909 reforms)?
o: Both made identical commitments regarding self-government
Morley had promised immediate self-government while Montagu withdrew that promise
Montagu rejected any form of Indian participation in administration
Montagu explicitly made self-government a government policy goal, unlike Morley who had rejected any move towards parliamentary government in India

q: Indian nationalist objections to Montagu's August 1917 statement centred on which two concerns?
o: The statement's silence on separate electorates
The statement's promise of immediate full independence, which nationalists found unrealistic
The complete absence of any mention of self-government
The absence of a specific timeframe, and the government alone deciding the pace and nature of advance towards responsible government
